articles.title: Democratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian elections
articles.summary: Legislators sent letter to Marco Rubio saying US interference is weakening Brazil’s democratic institutions
articles.byline: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: A group of 31 Democratic members of the US Congress has sent a letter to the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, criticising the Trump administration over “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections.

Latin America’s largest country will hold the first round of its presidential election on 4 October, with polls showing a technical tie between the incumbent leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro.

In the letter sent to Rubio on Thursday, 30 members of the House of Representatives and the senator Bernie Sanders listed a series of measures the US government took that they interpret as attempts to secure a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.

They wrote that those actions “reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America”, citing the recent midterm elections in Argentina and presidential elections in Honduras and Colombia.

In July, a group of 11 Democratic members of Congress sent a similar letter arguing that Trump was trying to interfere in Colombia’s election in favour of the far-right millionaire and former lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who went on to win the second round.
In Thursday’s letter, the lawmakers wrote that US officials under Trump have engaged in a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil”.

They noted that when Trump imposed his first tariffs on Brazil last year, he made clear that one reason was Bolsonaro’s trial over his attempt to stage a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The former president was ultimately convicted and, unable to run because he is under house arrest, named his son to take his place.

They also cited new tariffs that Trump imposed on Brazil in July under section 301 of US trade law, as well as plans by the US government to send two officials to Brazil to “cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s voting system, considered by many experts to be among the most reliable in the world”. The Lula administration ultimately denied the US delegation visas.

The Brazilian president has repeatedly complained that Trump is trying to interfere in Brazil’s elections and, in his speech opening the UN general assembly this week, said, without naming anyone: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy, internal or external, to act against the will of the people.”
after newsletter promotion

In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US is “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.
They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October.
The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

articles.title: Rapper Macklemore announces 'Free Palestine' tour after Ed Sheeran fallout
articles.summary: Proceeds from the tour, which begins in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians, he says.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Macklemore performs at the Goldencoast Rap Festival in Corcelles-les-Monts, near Dijon, central-eastern France, on 30 August, 2026
Rapper Macklemore is launching a "Free Palestine" tour, days after being dropped from Ed Sheeran's Loop Tour following pro-Palestinian comments he made onstage earlier this month.
"So, as you all know, my schedule freed up a bit," he said upon announcing the tour on Thursday.
The American artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - said proceeds from the tour, which launches in Dublin next month, will go to organisations supporting Palestinians.

Macklemore's onstage comments and subsequent removal from the tour led Sheeran's support acts to drop out, while the British singer stressed that the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoter, not by himself.

In a statement on Thursday, the rapper said that the last couple of weeks had shown him there had been "a collective awakening around Palestinian liberation, the power of billionaires that try to censor that call, and what we expect from artists right now".

"What happened to me is bigger than one artist or one stage," he said. "When the billionaire class can decide which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear, everyone should be paying attention."
Macklemore said he had spent the last week contacting artists who had used their platforms to stand in solidarity with the Palestinian people, regardless of the consequences.
Due to how quickly the tour came together, several details were still being worked out, he added: "But this is a moment of momentum, and there is work to be done."
Macklemore's new tour will begin in Dublin on 26 October followed by Paris on 29 October and London on 30 October.
US dates will also be added, he said, with additional tickets going on sale next week.
"I cannot hide how I feel anymore": Ed Sheeran addresses Macklemore row at show

While performing as the opening act for Sheeran at a concert in early September in New Jersey, Macklemore said: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."
The Thrift Shop rapper then performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters at Columbia University.

After he was taken off the tour on 14 September, Macklemore accused stadium owners of rallying together to push him out. He was also accused by billionaire stadium owner Robert Kraft of hate speech and antisemitic rhetoric surrounding Israel and Gaza.
Sheeran early on said that the decision to drop Macklemore from his tour was made by concert promoter Messina Touring Group.
His early remarks led to all of his support acts to drop out of the tour in solidarity, and fans to express frustration. Ticket prices for the tour plummeted as well.
Sheeran addressed the controversy head-on during the start of his set in Philadelphia last week.
He said he had made "mistakes" handling the fallout, apologising to fans and taking a stand on the Israel-Gaza conflict, which he said was "a humanitarian issue".
He described the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks as "horrific", and also called the situation in Gaza "unjustifiable and disproportionate".

articles.title: DPWH seeks P20B 'institutional amendments' within proposed 2027 budget
articles.summary: The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is proposing institutional amendments worth around P20 billion to its proposed P643.95-billion budget for 2027, a House lawmaker said Thursday.

blocks.text: Published September 25, 2026 1:50am
The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is proposing institutional amendments worth around P20 billion to its proposed P643.95-billion budget for 2027, a House lawmaker said Thursday.
Surigao del Sur Rep. Romeo Momo Jr., who sponsored the DPWH budget in plenary, said the proposed amendments would realign funds for needed infrastructure projects.
DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon said among these projects are flood control and drainage improvement. He said the list of projects would be made public by the agency.
The proposed tweaks in the DPWH budget surfaced following the inquiry of ACT Teacher Party-list Rep. Antonio Tinio on Thursday's plenary deliberation of the proposed budget.
"Are there institutional amendments to the DPWH budget in the NEP (National Expenditure Program) proposal? ...What is the magnitude of this institutional amendment?" Tinio asked.
Momo replied, "Yes, there is, to be submitted, roughly P20 billion."
"There will be no additional; it will be within the budget of the DPWH," Momo added.
Asked what projects would be affected, the sponsor said some projects may be retained but their allocations could be reduced to accommodate the proposed realignments.
The sponsor also assured lawmakers that the proposed amendments would still undergo the required review and compliance, despite the changes being introduced after the NEP was submitted.
Tinio also pointed out that 80 percent of the budget for Capital Outlay (CO) of the agency was lodged in the central office.
"We notice it is highly centralized; 80 percent of CO, or around P603 billion, is with the central office. Only around P39 billion is with the district engineering offices," he said.
Momo explained that this was so as part of the reforms being implemented by the agency, adding that projects with a budget over P50 million are automatically lodged in the central office.

On Tinio's inquiry, Momo acknowledged that some projects with a budget of P50 million and below are also under the central office to speed up their implementation, such as the Daang Maharlika road network. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: France says EU’s ‘Made in Europe’ law should not include the UK
articles.summary:
‘If you’re not in the internal market, you don’t get the same protection,’ says French minister of policy designed to curb Chinese competition

France is leading a push to exclude the UK from…

blocks.text: France is leading a push to exclude the UK from the EU’s “Made in Europe” policy that could result in British companies losing out in the race to supply European countries with low-carbon technologies and electric cars.
The plans were raised by Andy Burnham when he met the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, on the sidelines of the UN general assembly earlier this week.

The policy, still under negotiation, aims to protect European companies from intense and “unfair” state-subsidised competition from China. But the government fears British companies risk being collateral damage and resolving the issue has become one of Burnham’s top priorities for the EU-UK relationship.

One key EU proposal is the Industrial Accelerator Act, which would require authorities spending public money – awarding subsidies or public contracts – to favour European products in sectors such as renewable technologies and electric cars.
But there is an intense debate inside the EU on how to define “made in Europe” and how far to include countries such as the UK, Canada and Japan.
At a meeting of EU industry ministers in Brussels on Thursday, France pushed for a narrow definition, starting with the EU27.

“European taxpayers’ money should support [European] workers and European factories”, the French industry minister, Sébastien Martin, told reporters. Asked about the UK, he said: “The United Kingdom made a choice a few years ago to leave the European Union. That doesn’t mean that we don’t discuss things or that we don’t trade, it doesn’t mean that there can’t be agreements in certain sectors, but fundamentally there are those who have chosen the European project and those who have decided to leave.”

France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, speaking in London, had few assurances to offer the Burnham government either. Asked about the risks of pushing the EU’s like-minded trading partners away, Haddad said: “At the end of the day, if you are not part of the internal market and if you are not contributing to the financial capacity of the internal market, you don’t get the same kind of protection.”

Germany wants a broader “Made with Europe” policy that would include the UK and other allies. Germany’s economic affairs minister, Katherina Reiche, told her counterparts: “We must reduce unilateral and critical dependencies, but we must not isolate ourselves from the rest of the world. This means that partner countries must be included in the union-origin principle, in general and on the condition of reciprocity.”
This position gets broad support from Nordic countries, which traditionally favour open trade.

Sweden’s outgoing deputy prime minister, Ebba Busch, who leads on business policy, said “we always miss the Brits”. Sweden wanted “a good solution where there is balance, given that some European countries are not members of the European Union but still completely essential for a functioning European market” she added.

The charged internal EU27 debate on Made in Europe raises questions about the timing of the EU-UK reset summit, which was postponed when Keir Starmer stood down as prime minister. Since Burnham took office, no date has been fixed for the talks which are meant to happen in 2026.

British officials expect the summit will take place in November, although an earlier 6 November date has been scratched out. By December the EU is expected to be embroiled in deeply difficult internal negotiations on the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which are likely to consume the political bandwidth of EU leaders.
EU insiders believe that a Made in Europe agreement is a top priority for the UK, but have cautioned this cannot happen before the union has finalised its own position.

One EU diplomat said it was a “big risk” if the UK government were to insist on a deal at an autumn summit. “It puts [the UK] in a corner, because this [Made in Europe criteria] is a process that is very difficult for the EU27 [to agree internally]”.

Ireland, which is chairing EU ministerial negotiations, hopes for an agreement in December on the IAA, including the Made in Europe provisions, between the EU Council and the European parliament. “There are a divergence of views on the Industrial Accelerator Act, on European preference, on working with trusted partners and third countries,” said Ireland’s enterprise minister, Peter Burke. “It is difficult, but we have a pathway in sight.”

Poland’s economic development minister, Michał Baranowski, said it was too early to say whether countries such as Switzerland, the UK, Japan, Australia and Canada would be in or out, adding: “All these countries are in the mix of the discussion.”
The UK, he said, should have clarity on its status when the EU act is passed, he said, adding: “We are in the last stretch, but this last stretch might take a while.”
A UK government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.
“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”

articles.title: Launch of UK’s ‘largest AI supercomputer’ delayed by power supply problems
articles.summary:
Datacentre hailed by government was supposed to start operating next year but may be held back into mid-2030s

A huge datacentre project hailed by the UK government will miss its launch date…

blocks.text: A huge datacentre project hailed by the UK government will miss its launch date next year and could be delayed into the mid-2030s.
The site in Loughton, Essex, was described as the country’s largest AI supercomputer when it was announced in 2025, but power supply problems mean it now faces a lengthy wait before coming online.
Doubts had already emerged about the scheme after the Guardian revealed in March that the planned location was still an operational scaffolding yard.

Now there are further concerns about the project due to its inability to obtain enough power before its planned 2027 debut. The Loughton supercomputer is being built by Nscale, a UK-based startup seeking a $35bn (£26bn) flotation this year.

UK Power Networks (UKPN), the company that will connect the site to the local power grid, has reportedly told Nscale the grid will not be able to supply sufficient power to the datacentre until the early to mid-2030s.
The power delay was first reported by Morning Intelligence, an AI industry newsletter.

Nscale said it was “committed to the project” but the failure tofind a quick fix to the power supply issue underlines how much energy has become a hindrance to datacentre development. The scaffolding yard site has now been cleared by Nscale, however. The company is also investigating whether it can generate power onsite and whether it can speed up the connection process.

Keir Starmer’s government cited the Loughton project when announcing the UK’s AI strategy in 2025, describing the site as the “largest UK sovereign AI datacentre”. Datacentres are the central nervous system of AI technology such as chatbots.

blocks.caption: The scaffolding company, which was operating on the site. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ofgem, the energy industry regulator, has warned of a logjam in applications for electricity connections. In June, it revealed there were 315 datacentres queueing to connect to the National Grid, representing 73GW of demand – compared with the peak energy demand for the entire country of 45GW.
The Loughton site is seeking up to 90MW of capacity, equivalent to the energy consumption of about 315,000 homes.

UKPN said it could not comment on an individual project. Schemes with large energy demand also require work to be done at a National Grid level, in order to ensure that energy demands can be met properly.

“In general, many datacentres, whilst they will connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the wider national electricity transmission network before they can begin operation,” said a UKPN spokesperson.

National Grid said: “We’re continuing to work closely with NESO [the government-owned National Energy System Operator], distribution network operators and customers to identify opportunities to accelerate connections where possible and support economic growth.”

articles.title: After several difficult years, economists now expect German economy to grow
articles.summary: Germany's economy is growing again, but recovery remains on shaky ground. High government spending is keeping the economy afloat, while energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers and debt continue…

image.caption: Leading economists presented their forecast with a bit of optimismImage: Sebastian Gollnow/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: After several difficult years, the German economy has regained its footing. Leading economic research institutes now expect the economy to grow by 1.3% in 2026 and by 1.1% next year. That is significantly more than was forecast back in the spring.

As to the reasons behind this, economists have pointed first and foremost to the global economy. Despite the war in the Persian Gulf, they say, the economy is proving surprisingly robust. "This is benefiting the German export sector, and underlying this is also the global boom in artificial intelligence," said Oliver Holtemöller of the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research in Halle during the presentation of the latest report in Berlin.

Because of the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has cut off supplies from competitors, German companies have seen increased demand from abroad for petroleum and natural gas-based chemical products, for example.

In addition, the construction of AI data centers is driving demand for German companies. Some examples include machinery for energy production and services related to information and communication. Government spending on infrastructure and defense is also a significant driver of this upswing.
German industry shifts to defense production amid job losses

However, researchers believe it will not last. For 2028, the institutes expect growth of only 0.4%. "The drivers of growth will continue to dwindle," said Stefan Kooths of the Kiel-based research institute IfW. High energy prices, a shortage of skilled workers, an aging population and years of low investment by many companies are slowing growth. The institutes therefore warn against misinterpreting the latest positive figures as the beginning of a new economic boom.
Upturn fueled by debt

In this situation, the federal government is also playing a decisive role. The coalition of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) has decided to invest heavily in modernizing infrastructure and the Bundeswehr.

In the short term, this additional spending is also helping generate business for companies and safeguard jobs. At the same time, investments in roads, railways, digital networks and military equipment should strengthen Germany's competitiveness.

Economic analysts agree that this spending has had a positive effect on the economy. Especially at a time when consumers are tightening their belts and many companies are postponing investments, the government has been an important engine of growth. But this is also where economists are raising concerns. That's because the spending is financed through debt.

According to forecasts, the government deficit will rise from 4.1% of GDP this year to 4.7% in 2028. At the same time, the government's interest burden will grow. Future budgets will have to allocate an ever-larger share of funds to servicing debt.

"We have two major challenges: one is demographics, and the second is energy security and energy prices," said Holtemöller. In this context, the economist from Halle sharply criticized what they see as a lack of clarity regarding "the measures, reforms and regulatory framework" that Germany aims to use to phase out fossil fuels. They note that a vision for how the energy transition could be carried out in accordance with the Climate Protection Act is "not even vaguely" outlined.
Is Germany's weak economy boosting the right-wing AfD?
AfD's success is scaring off skilled workers

Germany's greatest challenge remains the declining labor force. As the baby boomers enter retirement, the economy is losing millions of workers. Many industries already complain of labor shortages. There needs to be greater openness "to the immigration of skilled workers," said Holtemöller.

Referring to the electoral successes of the anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) — a party that is, in part, right-wing extremist — Holtemöller cited studies indicating that "regions where populist parties are in power tend to have weaker economic growth than other regions." Openness, he emphasized, is the most important factor.

If immigration remains low, the average age of the population will only increase. This will drive up the cost of social security contributions, which in Germany are evenly split between employees and employers. On pension reform, economists are calling for doing away with the option to retire early after 45 years of contributions without any reduction in benefits. They argue that the debate about moving away from this policy is misguided.
What are the German government's pension, labor reforms?
The economy in transition

While the government is mobilizing billions, the private sector's momentum is lacking in many places. Investors are being deterred "because they don't know what to expect or what the business landscape looks like here," Kooths explained.

"What companies need now are not new debates but decisions on economic policy," demanded Helena Melnikov, chief executive of the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry. "This can only be achieved through a decisive course of reform: cutting costs, reducing bureaucracy, streamlining procedures and modernizing infrastructure."

For many decades, Germany was a country with a strong industrial sector. But that sector continues to shrink. About 15,000 industrial jobs are lost every month. Particularly hard-hit are industries such as automotive, mechanical engineering and metals. At the same time, the past two years have seen the emergence of many startups in the fields of digitalization and AI.

But according to economists, these new companies lack support, particularly when it comes to financing. As a result, many are relocating to the US. "We're very good at things like development, patent applications and so on, but the problem is that the ideas developed here end up creating value elsewhere," noted Timo Wollmershäuser of the ifo Institute in Munich.
Volkswagen crisis: Emden plant closure impacts whole region

When asked what could further improve growth prospects in Germany, the researchers pointed to a catalog of reforms that was presented last spring. The proposals include, among other things, a cap on social security contributions and stronger work incentives for older workers. As for the energy transition, the institutes place greater emphasis on price signals and advocate against taking national action on climate protection without other countries.
Notable criticism was directed at the fuel rebate scheduled to take effect on October 1. Researchers said it amounts to a blanket handout for which there is insufficient fiscal leeway.

The government cannot currently afford such expensive measures, and they are "also economically counterproductive," said Oliver Holtemöller. Cutting fuel taxes would "undermine efforts to reduce demand, which is precisely what is needed when energy supplies are tight."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: N.S. teacher charged with sexually assaulting student at school
articles.summary: Matthew Donahoe, 53, faces charges in incidents alleged to have occurred this school year. RCMP have identified other victims and say there may be more.

image.caption: Matthew Donahoe appeared at Pictou provincial court on Thursday, Sept. 24. 2026. (Luke Ettinger/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·Updated
Matthew Donahoe, 53, faces charges in incidents alleged to have occurred this school year. RCMP have identified other victims and say there may be more.
Matthew Donahoe, 53, faces charges including sexual assault and administering a noxious substance

A Nova Scotia teacher is facing a slew of charges, including sexual assault involving a student at the school where he taught, and RCMP say they have identified other victims in similar alleged incidents.

Matthew Donahoe, 53, of Bible Hill, N.S., has been charged with sexual assault, sexual interference, assault with a weapon, two counts of assault by choking, four counts of assault, and administering a noxious substance.
RCMP said the charges relate to multiple victims, but would not say how many.
Police also would not share information about the age or gender of the victims, what grade Donahoe taught or whether the affected students were in his class.
Donahoe is a teacher at Dr. W.A. MacLeod Consolidated School in Riverton, N.S. The school serves students in pre-primary to Grade 8.
RCMP said they received an initial report of an assault on Sept. 10, just five days into the school year. During their investigation, they identified other victims of similar alleged assaults.
All the alleged assaults occurred within the 2026-27 school year and took place inside the school, during the school day, RCMP said.
According to police, the Chignecto Central Regional Centre for Education removed Donahoe's access to the school and students at the time of the initial allegation of an assault.
In a statement, the regional education centre said the charges are "deeply troubling" and it takes the matter "very seriously."
The centre had supports available at the school on Thursday and will continue to do so into next week. The school has notified families that Donahoe has been placed on leave, the statement said.
RCMP said there may be more victims, and said investigators will use a supportive and trauma-informed approach to investigating.
"Investigators understand that coming forward may be difficult," Cpl. Carlie McCann told CBC News.

"We want you to understand that we can go at the pace and use the process that is going to work for you or your loved ones or the people you care for and we understand that this maybe a difficult thing for people to bring forward."
McCann said victims can come forward to police without deciding immediately if they want to be involved in the full investigation or court process. She said resources are available to help.

items: More stories from Northern Nova Scotia

blocks.text: Donahoe was arrested Wednesday.
He appeared in Pictou provincial court on Thursday afternoon with a white beard and collared shirt. Families of students also attended court.
Some of Donahoe's release order conditions include:

items: No contact with persons under age 18.
He's not allowed to attend places youths frequent.
He has to abide by a curfew.
He must reside with a surety in Dartmouth, N.S.
Attending court when directed.
Remaining in Nova Scotia.
Not being within 500 metres of any home, school or workplace of 10 named individuals.
Not possessing any weapons.

Not attending any public park, school ground, daycare centre, swimming pool, playground, skating rink, community centre, recreation centre or anywhere persons under the age of 18 are present or might reasonable be expected to be present.

blocks.text: Donahue is due back at court on Oct. 19.

articles.title: Justice minister says miscarriage of justice likely occurred in Sask. murder case, orders new appeal
articles.summary: A new appeal has been ordered for Neressa and Odelia Quewezance, who were convicted by a jury in 1994 of second-degree murder in the death of Anthony Joseph Dolff.

image.caption: Neressa Quewezance, left and her sister Odelia Quewezance outside of the Court of King's Bench in Yorkton in late 2020. On Thursday, Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser ordered a new appeal to be heard in their case. (Dayne Patterson/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
A new appeal has been ordered for Neressa and Odelia Quewezance, who were convicted by a jury in 1994 of second-degree murder in the death of Anthony Joseph Dolff.
Neressa and Odelia Quewezance convicted by jury in 1994
The federal minister of justice has ordered a new appeal in the case of two sisters who were convicted of murder more than 30 years ago.

The appeal was announced on Thursday, after an "in-depth" review by the ministry that took more than four years and found "reasonable grounds to conclude that a miscarriage of justice likely occurred."
Odelia and Neressa Quewezance, sisters from Keeseekoose First Nation in Saskatchewan, were convicted in 1994 of second-degree murder in the death of Anthony Joseph Dolff, a farmer from Kamsack, Sask.
"My decision does not decide guilt or innocence, as that will rest with the courts," Justice Minister Sean Fraser said in a news release.

items: Sask. woman who spent 30 years in prison system struggling with freedom

blocks.text: "Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts for new information to be considered."
The new information was not before the courts at the time of the sisters' trial or appeal, the government said.
After 30 years bail hearing begins for Quewezance sisters who say they were wrongfully convicted
In an emailed statement, Odelia Quewezance spoke on behalf of herself and her sister and thanked everyone who has "kept the faith" with them over the years.
"Neressa was 18 when she was arrested and is now 52. I was 21 and am now 55. But we have never stopped fighting," Odelia said.
"Today’s announcement by the minister is encouraging and now we will continue the fight in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal."
The murder
On Feb. 25, 1993, Dollf invited the two young Indigenous girls and their 15-year-old cousin to his home in Kamsack, Sask.

Both girls had attended residential school and were victims of institutionalized violence, their lawyers have said. Dolff had worked at the St. Phillips Residential School on Keeseekoose First Nation.
Events that night led to Dolff's death. The 15-year-old cousin confessed to stabbing him.
Odelia and Neressa were also charged with murder.

items: Indigenous sisters hope for exoneration after almost 30 years in prison system

blocks.text: "They were held in the Kamsack RCMP detachment for five days, despite a judge's order that they be taken to a detention centre," a news release from Innocence Canada said. "RCMP officers claimed that Odelia and Neressa confessed over five days of questioning to being involved in Mr. Dolff's stabbing."
Both were convicted of second-degree murder after a trial in Yorkton Court of King's Bench.

David Milgaard brought the sisters' cases to Innocence Canada, a non-profit organization that advocates for the exoneration of people who have been wrongly convicted. It filed an application with the justice minister on Dec. 21, 2021, asking for the review.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico regain access to White House
articles.summary: A federal judge has ordered President Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS NOW and Politico after he banned the media outlets from the premises. Hours later, the media announced they had…

image.caption: A judge has ordered that Trump's White House ban on three media outlets be liftedImage: Alex Wroblewski/AFP

blocks.text: CNN, MSNBC, and Politico journalists were allowed back in the White House on Thursday, hours after a federal judge said US President Donald Trump must lift his ban on journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico accessing the White House.
The ruling came in response to a lawsuit filed by the news organizations contesting the ban, which was issued on September 18.
In his order, District Judge Tim Kelly said the ban was likely unconstitutional.
Kelly said his order must remain in place for 14 days.

"This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law," Theodore Boutrous Jr., attorney for the outlets, said in a statement emailed to the AP news agency. "We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action."
On Thursday morning, journalists from three affected media outlets were initially denied access. However, later in the day, the media announced they had been granted access to the White House.
What did the judge say about the ban?
Kelly rejected the government's claim that national security concerns promoted the ban.

"The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs' hard passes will ​in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation ​proceeds," he said.
He pointed out that Trump himself had initially cited only an "alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity" in reporting by the outlets as the reason for the ban.

At a Wednesday hearing, Kelly said two previous rulings from the US Court of Appeals for the ⁠District of ​Columbia Circuit had established that White House press passes can be revoked only after due process.
He said the banned news outlets did not appear to have been given a proper chance to contest the ban.
Kelly, who was nominated by Trump in 2017, ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018.
The ban has led other media outlets, including DW, to take action in solidarity by suspending pooled coverage of Trump events.
Department of Justice support for ban

On Tuesday, the Justice Department had argued in a filing that access ⁠to the White House was a privilege, not ​an entitlement, and that the president had the authority to deny access news organizations.

The outlets, in turn, argued they were singled out because of the content of their coverage and called the ban a "blatant violation" of the First Amendment, which prevents government infringement on freedom of speech and freedom of the press in the United States.

articles.title: Carney government is inconsistent in how it labels spending, budget watchdog says
articles.summary: Ottawa's fiscal watchdog says the way the Liberal government defines certain types of spending in its new budget framework can be inconsistent and contradictory.

image.caption: Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan is seen in June. Her office released a report on Thursday saying the way the federal government categorizes federal spending is inconsistent. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
Ottawa's fiscal watchdog says the way the Liberal government defines certain types of spending in its new budget framework can be inconsistent and contradictory.
Prime minister says government is on track to balance its operating budget next year
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 24, 2026 12:39 PM EDT | Last Updated: 19 minutes ago
The Liberals under Prime Minister Mark Carney introduced a new budget framework that divides spending between day-to-day operating expenses and measures to stimulate capital investment.

A new report from the Office of the Parliamentary Budget Officer argues the way Ottawa defines those categories isn't as stringent as the definition used in other jurisdictions like the United Kingdom.
For example, two similar programs at Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada that are both aimed at spurring investments in farm equipment are classified differently under the framework.

items: Liberals on better-than-expected ground, plan to spend billions on skilled trades in economic update

blocks.text: Carney said last week the federal government is on track to balance its operating budget next year — but the budget office's projections, based on figures from the spring, anticipate Ottawa hitting that fiscal anchor two years later.

John Fragos, spokesperson for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, says the government is sticking by its pledge to balance the operating budget a year early and the upcoming fall budget will demonstrate Ottawa's fiscal prudence.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Craig Lord is a reporter with The Canadian Press.

articles.title: Police arrest far-right activist Daniel Thomas after ‘dinghy slashed in Channel’
articles.summary:
Thirty-seven-year-old in custody on suspicion of crimes including criminal damage with intent to endanger life

The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been…

blocks.text: The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was onboard.

The arrest came as the Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year. Responding to the figures, the government said it would “push further and harder” to crack down on the people organising the crossings.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man of no fixed abode had been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder onboard was damaged in the Channel. The man was arrested “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety”.

He was also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals”. Police said he remained in custody on Thursday.

The force had earlier said it was looking at footage livestreamed by Thomas, in which he could reportedly be seen using a knife to stab and slash an inflatable dinghy in the middle of the Channel after asylum seekers had been helped to safety but a French rescue worker had just got onboard.

Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of the dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on to the larger boat.

Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.

blocks.caption: The far-right activist Daniel Thomas in London this month. Photograph: Carl Court/Getty

blocks.text: A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform.

The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence, and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.

Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.
Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

The latest Home Office figures put renewed focus on the government’s handling of small boat arrivals in the UK. A government spokesperson said: “Our progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable, with crossings down by 42% and the lowest recorded over the summer months since 2020. But this week’s events show that while the peaks we are seeing are far below those of previous years, we need to push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade.”

Wednesday’s arrivals take the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565. Home Office data indicates this is down 42% on this time last year (32,188) and 26% below the figure at this stage in 2024 (25,165).

This week ministers have also been concerned by two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days. Most small boats carrying asylum seekers to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025.

The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time,” after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”
On Thursday a 42-year-old man was jailed after throwing a plastic bottle at a police line and swearing at officers during an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.

Del Somerville, of Paulsgrove, was sentenced at Portsmouth crown court to two years in prison having previously pleaded guilty to the charge of violent disorder. He is the first to be sentenced over violence that erupted after the arrival of a small boat in the Hampshire city on 6 September.

Judge Daniel Sawyer told him his sentence would act as a deterrent to others after subsequent protests in the area. Describing Somerville as a “thug”, he told the defendant: “Police officers dedicate their lives to the protection of the public regardless of their own views, the very least they can expect is that those who engage in protests treat them with respect and the courts punish those who assault them.”

articles.title: Greek PM urges UK PM to return Elgin Marbles permanently
articles.summary: Andy Burnham said in 2023 the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

blocks.text: The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.
Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".
The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.
The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external.
"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.
Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.
This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".
Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".
British ambassador Lord Elgin was granted permission by the Ottoman Empire, the governing authority in Athens at the time, to remove some of the marble statues in the early 19th Century.
They were created between 447BC and 432BC to decorate the Temple of Athena - what is now known as the Parthenon, in the Acropolis in Athens.
After an 1816 parliamentary select committee deemed Elgin's actions legal, the sculptures entered the British Museum collection by an act of Parliament.
The Greeks dispute their removal was lawful and the demands to return the statues have been vocal.
The Parthenon gallery in the Acropolis Museum in the Greek capital was deliberately designed with spaces left for the sculptures in the British Museum.
Back in 2023, George Osborne, then the museum chair, told the BBC he was looking for a "more co-operative arrangement" after "quite a bitter disagreement" with the Greeks for more than 200 years.
Mitsotakis's latest comments appear to suggest a ramping up of rhetoric around the thorny issue once again.
Last month, Greece's health minister told Breitbart News he would like to see US President Donald Trump pressure the British to return the Parthenon pieces.
The British Museum's position - and that of the UK government - is that the law prevents the permanent return of items held in its collection, though loan agreements are common.
Campaigners point out that the British Museum Act could be amended. However, the UK government has not signalled that this is a priority.

articles.title: Volkswagen subsidiary delays opening of $7B St. Thomas, Ont., battery plant to 2029
articles.summary: PowerCo, the Volkswagen subsidiary building a $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than…

image.caption: This aerial drone photo shows construction underway at the site of the future PowerCo plant in St. Thomas, Ont. Its opening has been delayed until 2029, Volkswagen says. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: London

PowerCo, the Volkswagen subsidiary building a $7-billion electric vehicle battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.
Conservative MP raises concerns about delay, citing federal subsidies and job promises

The Volkswagen subsidiary building an electric vehicle (EV) battery "gigafactory" in St. Thomas, Ont., says the facility is now expected to begin operations in 2029, two years later than originally planned.
PowerCo Canada made the announcement in a news release about hiring Mississauga, Ont.-based EllisDon Corporation as the general contractor for construction of the factory.

"St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve," said a news release.
PowerCo declined to make a spokesperson available for an interview with CBC News about the delay.

items: Volkswagen to open its first North American EV battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont.

blocks.text: Originally scheduled for a 2027 opening, the $7-billion factory — with a promise of up to $13 billion in subsidies from the federal government — was first announced in 2023. It was estimated it would result in the creation of 3,000 direct jobs and tens of thousands of indirect jobs in the region.

items: Highway 3 expansion gets underway as St. Thomas prepares for battery plant boom
Construction has started on massive Volkswagen battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont.

blocks.text: To prepare for the arrival of the plant, surrounding municipalities and the provincial government have undertaken infrastructure projects to increase sewer and road capacity for the population boom that was expected in 2027.
Before the plant was announced, the province allowed St. Thomas to annex land from the neighbouring municipality of Central Elgin to make room for the development.
In August 2025, PowerCo Canada announced it had awarded two major construction contracts for the project. Construction began in October 2025, with work starting on the foundations for the facility.
St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston, who has championed the factory as a major driver of economic growth for his city, told CBC News he's unfazed by the two-year delay.
"They've picked a great local Canadian general contractor and in doing so, they had to adjust the [opening] date," said Preston.

items: PowerCo begins hiring blitz for positions at St. Thomas EV battery gigafactory

blocks.text: PowerCo has been hiring workers in the St. Thomas area since August 2025. Preston estimates roughly 500 people are currently employed by the company in the surrounding area.

He also cited "the number of employees they already have working and living in the city of St. Thomas, the amount of construction that's going on in that site each and every day" as reasons for maintaining confidence in the project.
Preston also pointed to Yarmouth Yards, a large industrial park developed by St. Thomas, which is being populated by industries that are complementary to battery production.
Provincial officials also welcomed EllisDon's selection as general contractor.

In a written statement to CBC News, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade said the contract "represents a major milestone as they work towards the start of production that will create thousands of direct and indirect jobs across the supply chain."
The ministry's statement didn't address the two-year delay.

"We look forward to continuing to work with PowerCo as they progress on their $7-billion gigafactory in St. Thomas that will position Ontario at the forefront of innovative battery and automotive production for decades to come," it said.
Area MP raises concerns
Andrew Lawton, the Conservative MP representing Elgin—St. Thomas—London South, called news of the delay disappointing and questioned Volkswagen's commitment to the plant.

“I realize that Volkswagen is saying it's just about pace and not about the overall commitment. But ultimately, it is about the commitment because we were expecting this to be moving forward at a speed that we're just not seeing,” Lawton said.
Lawton also said he wants to know what the federal government is doing to move things along and ensure Volkswagen remains committed.

"We saw $13 billion worth of federal subsidies put forward to this and the promise — the expectation — was 3,000 well-paid local jobs, not to mention the construction jobs. All of this has been thrown into jeopardy right now."
EV market shifts affect Ontario auto plans
The market conditions cited by PowerCo come as automakers across Ontario have adjusted plans for electric vehicle production amid changes in EV demand.

In April 2025, General Motors cited lower-than-expected demand when it announced plans to halt production of the Chevrolet BrightDrop electric delivery van at its CAMI Assembly plant in Ingersoll. Hundreds of workers were laid off.

items: Hundreds of workers laid off at Ingersoll, Ont., assembly plant as GM halts production
Honda more definitively halting $15B EV plant development in Ontario, according to reports

blocks.text: Honda also delayed plans for a $15-billion EV plant in Alliston in 2025 before ultimately cancelling the project. The company said it would continue to assess the EV market.
At the same time, Canadian EV sales have shown signs of growth.
Statistics Canada data released in June showed the number of new EVs purchased by Canadians had increased by more than 20 per cent compared with the same period a year earlier.
Canadians bought 8,672 new EVs in January, 12,547 in February and 21,574 in March before sales fell to 17,795 in April.

articles.title: Houthi advances in Yemen drive displacement, deepen humanitarian crisis
articles.summary: With more than 132,000 people already displaced by the latest fighting and Houthi territorial gains, Yemen is on the brink of slipping back into a full-fledged humanitarian emergency. DW spoke with…

image.caption: The conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government has prompted a humanitarian displacement crisis which is compounded by a lack of aid fundingImage: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mohammed Musleh is still in shock. Following the Houthi capture of the port town of Mokha earlier in September, his family had to flee their home without time to pack.

"We have no idea what will happen now," the 46-year-old told DW. His wife, Muna, is also worried, as the family couldn't bring their personal identification documents. "The Houthis told us to leave, basically immediately. We had no time to take anything," she said.

For now, the family and their two young daughters are staying with relatives in Aden, the largest city controlled by the government in southern Yemen. "We tell our kids in the meantime that we hope to return home soon," the couple said.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of the Presidential Council, the leadership body of Yemen’s internationally recognized government, said that recent battlefield changes would not alter the government's goal of restoring state authority nationwide.
However, given the latest advances by the Iran-backed Houthis and their territorial gains in Yemen, a return of the Musleh family to their home in Mokha is unlikely for now.

Since late July, the Iran-backed Houthis have expanded their areas of control from the north and center of the country to much of Yemen's Red Sea coast, seizing territory from forces of the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed government. The conflict continues to escalate, along with an exchange of missile and drone attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis are currently pushing further into the country toward the strategic Kahboub Mountains. The mountain range is significant as it overlooks areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key waterway that had been serving as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid Iran's blockade of the nearby Strait of Hormuz.
Staying at home or leaving Taiz?
The mountains are also only around 40 kilometers (25 miles) southwest of Taiz, which is under government control.

blocks.caption: Yemeni government forces and Houthi forces are fight over control of the strategic Kahboub Mountains near Taiz Image: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Fatima, a mother in Taiz, has been telling her children that the sounds of shelling are from fireworks. "We are scared and we are also worried as gas has already become unavailable and prices are rising. Merchants are no longer coming into Taiz," she told DW, asking not to publish her full name for fear of reprisal.

Rania and her children have also decided to stay at home in Taiz for now. "But we fear that if the Houthis tighten their grip on the city of Taiz, we will find ourselves under siege again," she said. She also doesn't want to use her first name, and vividly recalls the "suffocating blockade of 2015 and 2016, when the entry of food and goods was cut off."

During the previous war between the Iran-aligned Houthi group and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, which began in 2014 and largely ended with a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022, Houthi forces blocked most routes into the government-controlled city of Taiz for almost two years. The restrictions on food, medical supplies and humanitarian aid drove up prices and left people on the brink of famine.
Growing displacement numbers

The World Health Organization said this week that at least 674 people have been killed and 2,998 injured since fighting escalated in August. However, due to the ongoing clashes, the death tally may already be higher, as fighting is ongoing.

The conflict has also prompted mass displacement of more than 132,000 people, according to the International Organization for Migration. In recent days, more than 90,000 people found refuge in Aden, Lahj, Abyan and Al Dhale'e governorates and even in Marib, the UN refugee agency's Yemen representative Armen Yedgaryan saidon Tuesday.
He also predicted that intensifying fighting could drive more mass displacement, with growing numbers of people expected to flee to Djibouti, Somalia and other countries, as well as within Yemen.

blocks.caption: According to the IOM, at least 132,000 people have been displaced, and numbers are likely to grow in the coming period of the conflictImage: IOM Djibouti/AFP

blocks.text: "Conditions for displaced people are increasingly severe as they arrive at already congested displacement sites in urgent need of shelter, food, clean water, healthcare and protection, placing additional pressure on fragile services and infrastructure," he said.

Even before the latest escalation, more than 5.2 million people were internally displaced in Yemen, and the current fighting is deepening an already dire humanitarian crisis in the country, the UN refugee agency added.
Around 22 million people require humanitarian assistance, including internally displaced people and around 65,000 refugees and asylum-seekers, mainly from Somalia and Ethiopia.

blocks.caption: The UNHCR's Yemen operation is only 18%  funded in 2026, leaving aid organizations without funds to respond to the latest escalationImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Displaced Yemenis help other displaced Yemenis

"I was in the Al-Kud site, a camp for internally displaced people or IDPs, in Abyan governorate on Sunday," Alison Bottomley, an advocacy adviser with the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) in Yemen, told DW. "317 families have arrived since the fighting began, increasing the number of people from 1,460 to 2,629 people," she said.
However, there is no funding to support them. "These IDPs are surviving purely off the generosity of other IDP families."

She told DW that she met Mustapha, a man who was displaced from his hometown of Mawza seven years ago during the previous war in Yemen. He has been living at the IDP site ever since. "He told us he was hosting 22 families in his shelter, all people from his hometown in Mawza. Together, they share a single latrine. When I asked how they were all eating, he said they share one meal together every other day."
Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi meanwhile released a video message in which he told Yemenis in western and southern provinces that they are not the target.
However, Yemeni political analyst Hisham Al-Omeisy said these are empty words.
"The Houthis may measure this offensive in kilometers gained and territory seized, but Yemenis are measuring it in homes abandoned, families torn apart, and lives lost," he told DW.

"There is something profoundly cruel about pursuing military gains while ordinary Yemenis are once again being condemned to fear, hunger and displacement," Al-Omeisy said, adding that "the lines on the map may change, but the blood, grief and shattered lives behind those lines belong to real people. Yemen's civilians cannot continue to be treated as collateral damage in the Houthis' pursuit of power."
Yemen's conflict has displaced tens of thousands of people

articles.title: Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says
articles.summary:
Warning comes hours after Poland says fire at Starlink satellite station was ‘act of sabotage’

Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months,…

blocks.text: Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.

In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.
The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.

Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.

blocks.caption: The Starlink station in Wola Krobowska, Poland, April 2026. Photograph: Pleiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/Reuters

blocks.text: Gawkowski said it had not been established who ​was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack.
“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.
Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.

Earlier this month, Germany publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.

In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.

Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.
A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.

“Russian military top command is convinced some Nato countries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.
“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.

The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.
The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.

The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.
There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.

Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.
