articles.title: White House 'repeatedly violated' court order to restore press access, say media outlets
articles.summary: Employees from CNN, Politico and MS Now reported being denied entry, with some having passes confiscated.

blocks.text: Three US media outlets have requested an emergency court hearing, accusing the White House of having "repeatedly violated" a judge's order to restore their access in a stand-off with President Donald Trump.
Employees from CNN, Politico and MS Now reported being denied entry on Thursday morning, with some having their credentials confiscated, while others were granted access.
Judge Timothy Kelly ruled in the early hours of Thursday that Trump's ban on the outlets should be temporarily lifted because it "likely violated their constitutional due process rights".
Trump initially said he banned the outlets because of "fake news". The White House later cited national security.
It was unclear whether the refusal to admit some reporters on Thursday morning was because of an administrative lag as the White House potentially worked to comply with the judge's order.
The standoff was expected to impact TV coverage as Trump welcomes Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday morning ahead of a state dinner.
CNN said some of their journalists had been denied entry, including senior White House reporter Betsy Klein. But a producer was allowed to enter, the outlet reported.
Politico said one of its reporters was denied access to the White House and had his press credentials confiscated.
MS NOW reported that its White House reporter Laura Barrón-López and a producer were barred and had their passes taken, but another MS NOW producer was allowed in.
The White House is yet to comment on the ruling, and lawyers acting for the president may take further legal action.

articles.title: EU says Trump plan to ban US diesel exports would ‘negatively impact both sides’
articles.summary: US president’s suggested 90-day export ban before midterm elections could bring even higher fuel prices across Europe

blocks.text: The EU has warned Donald Trump against plans to ban US diesel exports to the global market, saying the move would negatively affect Europe and the US.
The European Commission has reacted with “concern” to reports this week that the US president could prevent diesel from reaching the global market.

Trump is reportedly considering a 90-day export ban to provide a temporary respite from high pump prices for US households before the midterm elections, after US diesel reached a record average of $6.52 (£4.93) a gallon. “I’ve ​said let’s not send ‌out the diesel. ‌We make a lot of diesel … I’ve called for it. ‌I’ve called for it within my people,” he said.

Olof Gill, a spokesperson for the EU’s executive arm, said on Thursday “any disruption would risk negatively impacting both sides” and the EU expected “close partners to consult each other before taking measures that affect shared markets”.

The EU made the diplomatic intervention as experts said that the potential export ban could be “devastating” for Europe, and traders scrambled to assess the continent’s reliance on imports from the US.
The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has warned that banning exports was a “blunt tool” that could harm US fuel supplies in the long term.

For Europe, the ban could be far more damaging. US diesel exports have made up a third of the continent’s imports this year, as supplies from war-damaged refineries in the Middle East and Russia have plummeted. By August, the US supplied about half of Europe’s diesel imports.
Pump prices have already climbed to record highs across Germany and the Netherlands, leading to calls for political leaders to protect households from rising costs.

blocks.caption: Diesel prices in some parts of the UK have passed £2 a litre  – and reached £2.17 a litre at BP Kinross Services in Perthshire, Scotland.  Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: In the UK, motorists may be only days away from fresh all-time highs, raising concerns over the economic impact of further price hikes for hard-pressed households. The RAC said the average cost of diesel was 197.75p a litre on Thursday, up from 142.38p before the start of the Iran war.

“A US export ban would be devastating for diesel supply in Europe, which would struggle to replace supply,” said Josh Michalowski, the head of European diesel pricing at Argus Media, a commodities data provider.

Fuel stations across Europe are unlikely to run dry, because Europe produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries. It also stores fuels in reserve. But experts fear that competing for cargoes on the global market would lead to higher market prices.

So far the market for diesel cargoes has remained relatively quiet since reports of a potential US diesel ban emerged this week, according to Benedict George, the head of European products at Argus. He said traders were still weighing up the degree to which the White House might limit US exports.

“If this prospect became even relatively serious [in the White House], it would be very serious for European markets. There would be some degree of panic given how reliant buyers have become on US cargoes,” George said. “There’s enough European diesel production to ensure that we wouldn’t run out, but losing US cargoes would mean buyers would have to compete with buyers in Asia for the few available cargoes from the Middle East and India, in what is already a very competitive global market.”
after newsletter promotion

The price of diesel has outpaced the rising price of global oil markets due to severe disruption to refineries in the Gulf and in Russia. The price difference – known as the “crack spread” – reached a record high earlier this month and could climb further still.

“A US ban on diesel exports would pose a significant challenge for the UK, given the country’s growing reliance on American refined fuel,” said Thomas Pugh, the chief economist at the audit, tax and consulting firm RSM UK.

blocks.caption: The Fawley oil refinery in Hampshire is one of only four remaining refineries in the UK. Photograph: Graham Mulrooney/Alamy

blocks.text: The UK has only four operating oil refineries after the closures of Grangemouth and Lindsey last year. Both produced diesel for the UK market. Pugh warned that losing almost 90,000 barrels a day of US distillate, or 18% of the country’s total consumption, would leave the UK even more exposed to global diesel prices. He added that, while shortages of fuel were unlikely immediately, a longer-term ban would make them a “real possibility”.
Although the number of motorists driving diesel passenger vehicles has fallen, it remains the lifeblood of the UK’s agricultural and logistics sectors by fuelling heavy machinery, lorries and vans.
The European Commission spokesperson said: “High-level contacts between the European Union and the US administration are ongoing.”
The UK government was contacted for comment.

articles.title: Who is Vic Rodriguez, petitioner vs. Sara Duterte impeachment vote threshold?
articles.summary: A former trusted ally of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is leading the charge against the Senate impeachment court's move that changed the 16-vote threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: A former trusted ally of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is leading the charge against the Senate impeachment court's move that changed the 16-vote threshold needed to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial.
Former Executive Secretary Vic Rodriguez has asked the Supreme Court to declare null and void the September 23 ruling of the Senate impeachment court in the trial of Duterte.

Rodriguez also asked for a temporary restraining order on the ruling, which lowered the base of the two-thirds vote needed to convict from all the members of the Senate to all the members who can legally and factually participate in the proceedings.
The former Palace official said the Constitution set the voting threshold at two-thirds of all the members of the Senate, which should be 16 if all 24 senators are counted.
Who is Vic Rodriguez?
Rodriguez served as Marcos' campaign spokesperson and chief of staff during the 2022 elections. Following Marcos' win, he became one of the earliest appointees to the Cabinet as Executive Secretary.

“Who can say no to President-elect Bongbong Marcos? It is an honor working with him, whom I have known for a very long time, and I believe he will serve the country efficiently and with unquestioned devotion. It is very flattering to work alongside the best person I’ve known,” he said.
However, in September 2022 or after just three months in office, Rodriguez announced that he stepped down as Executive Secretary. Back then, he said that he wanted to prioritize time with his family.

Things took a turn for the worse after he resigned from Marcos’ Cabinet, as the Partido Federal ng Pilipinas (PFP), the political party of the President, expelled Rodriguez from its ranks in November 2022.

The PFP said that Rodriguez was expelled for "incompetence as a public servant, conduct inimical to the interests of the party, abuse and breach of trust and confidence reposed on him by the President and the party, abandonment, and disloyalty."

In January 2024, Rodriguez joined local government officials and supporters of Duterte in a leaders’ forum in Davao City ahead of a prayer rally that will be held against the signature campaign to push for Charter change.
Rodriguez told GMA News Online that he was invited to be part of the leaders’ forum.
He also voiced his sentiment against the people’s initiative pushing for the amendment of the 1987 Constitution.
In October 2024, he filed his certificate of candidacy for senator. He said he will run as an independent.

In January 2025, Rodriguez, along with Davao City 3rd District Representative Isidro Ungab and others, asked the Supreme Court to declare the 2025 national budget as unconstitutional amid alleged irregularities and supposed blank items in the bicameral conference committee report.
Marcos has repeatedly said that there were no blank pages in the bicameral conference committee report on the 2025 budget.
During the “Tanong ng Bayan: The GMA Senatorial Face Off 2025,” in February 2025, Rodriguez explained the real reason why he had a fallout with the President.

“Hindi ko masikmura ang korupsyon kung kaya't ako ay umalis ng Malacañang. Ako ay binigyan pa ng isang posisyon, ang Presidential Chief of Staff, subalit hindi ko na gusto ‘yung direksyon na kanilang tinatahak. Kaya sabi ko, ayoko na at ako'y babalik na lang sa pribado,” Rodriguez answered.

(I could not stomach the corruption, that's why I left Malacañang. I was given one more position, the Presidential Chief of Staff, but I no longer liked the direction they were taking. So I said, I don't want to do it anymore and I'd just go back to private life.)

While he ran as an independent candidate in the 2025 elections, he was endorsed by PDP-Laban chairman and former president Rodrigo Duterte during the party’s proclamation rally on February 13, 2025 in San Juan City.
VP Sara Duterte impeachment

Ahead of the impeachment proceedings, in March 2026, Rodriguez joined several lawyers in asking the SC to issue a TRO to prevent the House of Representatives from proceeding with the impeachment complaints against Vice President Sara Duterte.

In a 186-page petition, the petitioners asked the SC to declare that the House Justice Committee gravely abused its discretion by sustaining the third and fourth impeachment complaints against Duterte, arguing they lacked sufficiency in form and substance.
They also asked the SC to declare that the third and fourth impeachment complaints should have been dismissed at the threshold for insufficiency in form and/ or substance.
On August 5, 2026, the SC dismissed the consolidated petitions, ruling that they are moot as the Senate impeachment court is already on its Day 13 of trial.

Rodriguez was born on December 12, 1973 in Quezon City. He finished his Bachelor of Laws at the University of Sto. Tomas. He took an Executive Education Program at the National University of Singapore.
According to his bio, he was elected barangay captain in 1994. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: 105-year-old investigated for crimes at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
articles.summary: The suspect is alleged to have been an accessory to murder at the Stalag 326 camp, where tens of thousands of Soviet PoWs died.

blocks.text: German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.
The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.
A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.
That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.

No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.

More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.
But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.

One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region.
Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.
Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.

articles.title: Why did an OpenAI system hack Australia's health system - and can it be stopped in the future?
articles.summary: News that an automated AI agent hacked a government IT system raises big questions about regulating the tech.
articles.byline: Henry Moore, Liv McMahon and Chris Vallance

blocks.text: The hack was carried out by an AI agent - an autonomous computer program that uses AI to complete a task with minimal human oversight.

On 18 June one of OpenAI's agents went rogue during a test exercise - the company has said it was supposed to "look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation".
In the process it "infiltrated" a private statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said.

OpenAI said it only realised the breach had happened at all in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity", and the company sent an email to a generic Australian government inbox some weeks later.
That email seems to have gone unnoticed for five days before it was escalated to Australia's cyber-security experts on 10 September.
The prime minister described the breach as "obviously unacceptable" and said OpenAI took "way too long" to inform Australian officials.
Analysts have also raised concerns over OpenAI's almost three-month delay in noticing and reporting the breach via email.
"The way the notice arrived bothers me as much as the delay," chief data and AI officer Simon Liu from cyber-security firm TrustDecision told the BBC.
Australia has said this incident is the first of its kind, and experts agree it might be.
As far as we know, hacks carried out by AI agents are still quite rare occurrences - but then again, it is largely up to companies themselves to disclose them.
Hacks like this have happened before. In July, OpenAI agents went rogue during a test and infiltrated tech start-up Hugging Face's internal systems.
The AI agents decided that ignoring the limits on what should be done to achieve their goal was the best course of action.
This is what the industry calls "misalignment" - broadly defined as when AI machines do not act in humanity's best interests, such as by bending the rules.
It is a problem that is fundamental to making AI safe, and it is proving challenging.

To put it simply, the type of AI models at play here - known as large language models - are designed to predict the likeliest output to a given input, rather than consider the consequences of that output as a human would.
Companies attempt to prevent negative consequences by placing "guardrails" on the AI but, as the Australian government found out, that is not always enough.

Dr Hammond Pearce, senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales Institute for Cyber Security, told the BBC this sort of hack would likely "grow in severity and in frequency", adding: "I do hope that this incident does start ringing alarm bells in governments around the world."

Niusha Shafiabady, professor of computational intelligence at the Australian Catholic University, said this incident had shown the need to "judge autonomous AI by its behaviour under pressure, not by the promises in a product launch".
"The deeper technical risk is that autonomous AI does not always know when it is wrong, and humans may not be able to see why it made a decision," she said.
"Without strong verification and hard boundaries, probabilistic errors can quietly become operational failures."
The explosive rise of AI has left governments scrambling to put protective measures in place, with some calling for companies to be forced to build ways to disable their own tech into its systems.
One idea backed by some AI firms and lawmakers is a "kill switch" - a way to simply to turn the tech off in a crisis.
OpenAI is reportedly, external already working to build automated tools which can shut down its systems if needed.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, former deputy prime minister and Facebook executive Sir Nick Clegg said the kill switch remains an unproven idea.
"There isn't a room with a little fuse box [where] you just pull out the fuse and everything winds down," he said, with AI tools underpinned by global infrastructure.
Cyber-security experts said the systems protecting Australia's Medicare were just not strong enough, and a skilled human hacker could have got around them.

But other experts say that is not the point - and that this was the latest case of AI agents ignoring laws around how to safely access online information, and perhaps the most serious yet given the information was under government control.

As warnings mount about the potentially devastating impact of AI, many in the industry and in governments around the world are openly wondering about what national and international regulations might be needed to keep it in check.
Meanwhile some scientists, experts and workers have dismissed the bleak projections as vague, hypothetical, or an effort by large AI developers to ensure their dominance.

As it stands, AI companies largely regulate themselves - but this week, 20 nations, including Australia and Canada, signed a joint statement calling for better safeguards, globally consistent standards, and an international regulator off the back of these concerns.

However, the US and China, two nations at the forefront of AI development, have so far resisted calls for greater regulation, raising questions over whether this hack will be the first of many, or the wake up call many experts want it to be.
"The immediate harm here appears limited, but the governance lesson is not," says Dr Raffaele Fabio Ciriello, senior lecturer in business information systems at the University of Sydney.

"As AI agents become more capable and autonomous, those capabilities need to be matched by proportionate containment, real-time monitoring, clear accountability, independent oversight, and much faster incident reporting."
Additional reporting by Tom Gerken and Joe Tidy

articles.title: Sobeys' parent Empire agrees to end property controls after battle with Competition Bureau
articles.summary: Canada's Competition Bureau has reached an agreement with Sobey's parent company to have the grocery giant strictly limit or stop using property controls after the agency found the practice to be…

image.caption: Shoppers are shown at a Sobeys grocery store in Toronto on June 26, 2023. The grocery chain's parent company, Empire Co. Ltd., will no longer enforce certain property controls after an agreement was reached with Canada's Competition Bureau. (Graeme Roy/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Business·New

Canada's Competition Bureau has reached an agreement with Sobey's parent company to have the grocery giant strictly limit or stop using property controls after the agency found the practice to be anti-competitive.
Deal means Empire Co. Ltd. will no longer be permitted to restrict competition through land titles

Property controls are clauses written into the land title that can prevent rival grocery stores from opening new stores nearby (exclusivity clauses), or can ban food products from being sold at nearby pet stores, dollar stores, gyms or other retailers and restrict what future leaseholders can sell on the land (restrictive covenants).

Empire Company Limited — which owns Sobeys, Farm Boy, Safeway, Freshco, IGA and others — has been under pressure from the consumer watchdog for months to get rid of their property controls after it found the practice to be anti-competitive.

"This all started with an investigation that we started in 2024 about the use of property controls by Loblaw and Sobeys and their impact in the grocery sector," said Anthony Durocher, acting senior deputy commissioner of the Competition Bureau.
"Loblaw has made commitments to curb its use," he told CBC News. "Now we have an agreement with Sobey's as well."
Win for consumers, economist says

The investigation into the Canadian grocery giants' use of property controls came off the back of federal committee hearings held in 2023 that were meant to get to the bottom of rising grocery prices.

"Sobeys, in a way, has been the hardest nut to crack," said economist Jim Stanford, who testified at those hearings. "They denied that these things were wrong and initially pledged to continue doing it."

items: How grocery giants control who can sell food in your neighbourhood
Competition Bureau looking deeper into how Sobeys can control who sells food in your area

blocks.text: The new deal is a win for the bureau — and for consumers, he said.
"I think this is a recognition that these practices are wrong — economically wrong and morally wrong — and the Competition Bureau is taking them seriously."

Land title documents obtained by the CBC's Marketplace earlier this year found stores within a radius of up to five kilometres from a grocery giant were restricted from selling perishable food items, like "fresh or frozen food, including meats, fruits, vegetables, fish, poultry, bakery, pre-packaged bread, delicatessen, bulk food or dairy products."
One reason why you might be paying more for groceries
Some restrictions also prevented nearby retailers, such as dollar stores, from offering steep discounts on big national brands like Kraft, Coca-Cola and Evian.

A spokesperson for Sobey's parent company, Empire, told CBC News in a statement that the company is "pleased to have resolved the matter of property controls with the Competition Bureau," adding that they continue to invest in their network of stores across Canada.

items: Canada's got a grocery competition problem. Are local food hubs the answer?

blocks.text: Empire Company Limited is the second-largest grocery network in Canada after George Weston Limited, which owns Loblaws, No Frills, Superstore, Zehrs, Dominion, Fortinos, Freshmart and others.

Loblaws committed to cease enforcing its own restrictive covenants and to limit its exclusivity clauses in 2025, after the Competition Bureau's initial probe. The watchdog says it continues to monitor that commitment.
'Exclusivity clauses' still permitted
While the new agreement legally requires Empire to refrain from using new or existing restrictive covenants, it does allow "limited" use of exclusivity clauses.
This means that while the company can no longer restrict what other businesses can sell, they can still prevent direct competitors from opening locations on a shared development.
"There are some cases where it's justified in specific circumstances," said Durocher, pointing to Competition Bureau's public guidance for retailers.

The guidance says a "limited" exclusivity clause can be pro-competitive in a scenario where "no retailer would otherwise make the necessary investments to become a key tenant in a new shopping plaza." It further states that in such a case, no retailers of a particular type would risk opening up in the shopping plaza without the exclusivity clause, "and so the clause increased competition."

The bureau is prepared to make case-by-case judgements in these instances, Durocher said, having identified 19 such scenarios on land occupied by Empire-owned grocery stores in the course of their investigation.
The federal government granted the Competition Bureau increased authority to enforce their property control rules earlier this year.
Ultimately, Durocher said, this makes it easier for grocers, butchers and bakeries to open up and to compete. "More competition means lower prices, more choice, more innovation," he said.

items: Competition Bureau to examine Canada's food supply chain
Ottawa has struggled to increase grocery competition. Will the new food strategy help?

blocks.text: Durocher said he intends to pursue similar, legally binding deals with other grocers, while simultaneously moving forward with the consumer watchdog's formal examination of the industry's barriers to competition launched in June.
This includes investigations into production and processing, transportation and distribution, and retail pricing across Canada's food supply chain.

As the examination continues, the Competition Bureau might be somewhat "hamstrung" by their limited powers, said Stanford, adding he would like to see more done to "stop these companies from getting so big in the first place."
"I'm encouraged by this, but I don't know if it means a whole new era of cracking down on food oligopolies or not," he said. "That remains to be seen."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Katie Pedersen is an investigative journalist for CBC Marketplace.

articles.title: Extremist parties are thriving ― and that scares people
articles.summary: Far-right and far-left parties are celebrating success after success, leaving moderate politicians in the dust and worrying many Germans. Political psychology helps us understand what's behind…

image.caption: The far-right AfD, seen here celebrating their win in Saxony-Anhalt, has won over many voters. For many others, however, their rise is cause for concern.Image: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: On September 6, Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt held elections for its state parliament. The big winner: The right-wing AfD (Alternative for Germany) party, which garnered 43.8% of the votes; more than ever before.
It's still unclear who will govern the state because the AfD does not have an absolute majority.
But it was a landslide win for the AfD, whose Saxony-Anhalt branch is classified as right-wing extremist by Germany's domestic intelligence agency, and that worries many Germans.

The day after the election, Chancellor Friedrich Merz from the conservative CDU said he was "deeply shocked" by the election results. "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany."
Merz's CDU lost more than half its share of the ballot compared to the last state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The CDU dropped from 37.1% in 2021 to 17.2% in 2026.
Two weeks later, at state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on September 20, the CDU didn't even make the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
It was the first time ever for the CDU; they got only 4.9% of the vote in the northeastern state. The strongest party was once again the AfD with 38.2%.

That same day, in the city state of Berlin, the socialist Left Party won the election and will likely govern Germany's capital. In Berlin, the CDU was the second-strongest party and the AfD came in third.
Why Germany's political center is losing ground
Germans worried about rise of far-right, far-left parties
These state elections show that parties on the extreme ends of the political spectrum are growing stronger in Germany.

The country has experience with both extreme right- and left-wing governments: the Nazis that led Germany into World War II and the Socialist Unity Party (SED) that ruled then-East Germany from 1949 until 1989.
A return to extreme politics is a scary proposition for some people.

In a representative monthly survey called "What worries the world?", the polling institute Ipsos found that almost one-fifth of Germans (18%) said they were worried by growing extremism in the country when they asked about 1,000 people between the ages of 16 and 74 years in March and April 2026.
Generally, people in Germany are concerned about where their country is going. In the Ipsos survey, 82% said they saw Germany as moving in the wrong direction.
How to measure a country's mood
Asking people about their fears or worries is just one way to take the nation's temperature.
But there are many ways to measure politically relevant emotions in the population.

Kerstin Pahl, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development in Berlin, told DW that possibilities include quantitative and qualitative surveys, as well as analyzing online discourse and the content people share on social media. It's also possible to read a nation's sentiment by observing real-life displays of emotions, like public protests and demonstrations.
For researchers like Pahl, it's also interesting to see how political issues can come to symbolize much more than their material or factual meaning.
"People may see their region's ailing infrastructure not just as proof of a lack of investment, but also as a sign that they have been forgotten [by their leaders]," said Pahl.
Affective polarization: Political opponents become the enemy
Extremist parties winning a higher percentage of the votes is what we see on the surface. Below that lie two kinds of societal polarization: Affective and ideological polarization.

"Affective polarization is a growing hatred for the political opponent. Most studies investigated this in the context of the US between supporters of the Democrat and the Republican Party," Eva Walther, head of the social psychology department at the University of Trier in western Germany, told DW. "When this happens on the party level, it's a problem."
MAGA moves to meddle in European politics
Politicians of different parties often have to work together and reach compromises. They don't need to like each other, but they should treat each other with respect, Walther said.
"When this respectful attitude starts crumbling, it's a problem for democracy," she added.
Ideological polarization: Which problem is the most pressing?
The other phenomenon, ideological polarization, is when society is split into distinct groups based on what issues people view as the most pressing problem for them.
For example, many people to the right of the political center in Germany see migration as the biggest problem, while many people to the left of the political center say it's the climate crisis.
When different crisis situations occur at the same time, such as migration and climate change, researchers refer to a "polycrisis."
Polycrises intensify ideological polarization, making it even harder for societies to find a common way forward.
"At the moment, we have the climate crisis overlapping with an affordable energy crisis, more of an economic problem," Walther said.

In the eyes of those for whom the climate crisis is the most urgent issue, fossil fuels should be abandoned as soon as possible. But for those most concerned with affordable energy, relying only on renewable energy sources would needlessly raise prices.

blocks.caption: What's the more urgent problem: climate change or the affordable energy crisis? The answer depends on where you fall on the political spectrumImage: Eckhard Stengel/imago images

blocks.text: People want politicians to take their problems seriously
The belief that a politician is competent and willing to tackle major challenges, to act, is a big factor in how much people trust democracy.
But that's also what makes overlapping crises so hard to manage: No matter which problems politicians attempt to solve first, one part of the population will be disappointed.
"Polycrises make it difficult for politicians to act, which means that people have less trust that politicians can solve the problems important to them," Walther said.
Right-wing extremist parties, however, aim to "satisfy people by giving them simplified answers to complex problems," added Walther.
This leads people to believe that extremist politicians can solve their problems ― which in turn leads to growing polarization.
But politicians from democratic parties can learn from clinical research to tackle this dilemma, according to Walther.
"When a person is in pain and goes to see a doctor, it's important that the doctor recognizes the patient's pain," she said.
Even if the doctor can't instantly solve the issue and make the pain go away, showing that they take the issue and the patient seriously is crucial. And the same goes for politicians.

"They need to make people's needs the first priority in their daily work," Walther said. "People want to be seen, so it's important for politicians to make it clear that they see and understand their problems."
Whether it's a doctor failing a patient or politicians failing the electorate, patient and electorate are likely to scream — and that's a signal we can all read.

articles.title: How renewed fighting in Tigray could spread across the Horn of Africa
articles.summary: Fighting has resumed in Ethiopia's Tigray region. In an interview with DW, Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.

image.caption: Tigrayan forces seized three local airports and launched attacks in Ethiopia's Afar and Amhara regions with allies there this weekImage: AFP

blocks.text: Fighting has erupted again in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive on September 23, with fighting also reported in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara.

The escalation threatens the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war between Ethiopia's federal government in Addis Ababa and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).
But the central question is bigger than the return of war to Tigray: could the conflict connect with the wars and rivalries already destabilizing the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?
Martin Plaut, British journalist and Horn of Africa expert, argues that the conflict could spill beyond Ethiopia's borders.

"If a conflict were to spill over, it is quite possible that a conflict involving Eritrea and Ethiopia could then involve Sudanese forces as well, which could drag the whole region into a war," he told DW in an exclusive interview.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again

Jalale Getachew Birru, a senior analyst for East Africa at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also stresses that the conflict cannot be viewed in isolation. ACLED is an independent conflict-monitoring and research organization that collects and analyses data on political violence and armed conflict around the world.
“The Ethiopia[n] case is not [an] isolated case for the Horn of Africa. It involves the neighboring countries as well, and it’s being displayed across the Horn of Africa countries," Birru told DW.

Her assessment points to a broader regional dynamic: Ethiopia's conflict is unfolding alongside shifting alliances and competing interests in neighboring Sudan and Somalia. ACLED's current analysis likewise places the renewed Tigray conflict within a wider pattern of instability across the Horn of Africa.
The risk is not based on a single regional alliance. It comes from the fact that several conflicts are already geographically and politically connected, Birru noted.
African Union urges restraint
The African Union (AU) also expressed deep concern about the possibility of further destabilization.
In a statement on September 23, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf warned that new political and military alliances risk reversing the progress made since 2020.

The AU called for an immediate end to actions that could escalate tensions, renewed direct talks under the Pretoria agreement and restraint by Ethiopia's neighbors. It also tasked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's High Representative for the Horn of Africa, with supporting diplomatic efforts.
The AU's intervention reflects concerns that the crisis could have wider regional implications, including the possibility that it could interact with conflicts beyond Ethiopia's borders.
Old enemies, new alliances

The TPLF recently joined six other Ethiopian armed groups in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Among them is the Amhara Fano movement, which fought against the TPLF during the previous war.

The alliance is not a unified military force. Its members have different political objectives and territorial interests. But its formation could leave the Ethiopian government facing several fronts at once.

The fighting in Afar, a northeastern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Djibouti, is particularly significant. The region contains the main transport corridor linking landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti, through which much of Ethiopia's international trade passes. Sustained fighting there could therefore threaten a vital economic lifeline.
And beyond Afar lies Eritrea.
Eritrea's potential role

During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. Since then, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara, Eritrea's capital, have deteriorated. Ethiopia's ambitions for access to the Red Sea have added to Eritrea's security concerns.
"The war could certainly escalate, and Eritrea could become involved," Plaut said.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups opposed to the government, while Asmara has denied such allegations. The extent of any direct Eritrean involvement remains difficult to establish independently.
Sudan: where conflicts could collide

Sudan has been at war since 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has drawn in regional powers and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises.
Plaut argues that Ethiopia and Eritrea are already indirectly involved on opposing sides.

"The Ethiopians are on the side of the RSF and Hemedti," he said, referring to its commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. "There has been strong evidence that there is a base in western Ethiopia which is supplying and training RSF fighters," Plaut added. DW has not independently verified that claim.
Explainer: How did Ethiopia's Tigray war start?
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has faced allegations of supporting the RSF, which it denies. Plaut identifies Eritrea, Egypt and Saudi Arabia as supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces.
"So both Eritrea and Ethiopia are already playing a role, indirectly, in the war," he said.

If Ethiopia and Eritrea were to enter direct hostilities, Sudan's rival forces could have incentives to exploit the new situation, Plaut noted. Fighting could put additional pressure on Sudan's eastern frontier and alter supply routes and military calculations.

Plaut sees the danger of a chain reaction: "Because you have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces, this could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."
"So the whole thing becomes a generalized conflict in the region," he said.
The Red Sea connection
The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

Eritrea and Djibouti lie on its western side, Yemen on the eastern side. The war in Yemen has already shown how insecurity around the Red Sea can disrupt international shipping and draw in outside powers.

Eritrea's location and its control of the port of Assab give it strategic importance far beyond Tigray. Any major deterioration in Ethiopia-Eritrea relations could therefore affect the wider security architecture of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also developed extensive political, economic and security interests across the Horn of Africa. Their interests overlap in some areas but diverge in others, particularly over Sudan.
The danger is escalation, not inevitability

None of this means that a regional war is inevitable. There is no evidence of a single military alliance stretching from Tigray to the Gulf. Ethiopia's armed groups have competing interests, Eritrea may avoid direct intervention, and Sudan's warring parties have their own priorities.
But conflicts do not need a common command structure to become interconnected.
Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds

The Tigray war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. The Pretoria agreement stopped the large-scale fighting, but many of the political and territorial disputes underlying the conflict remained unresolved.
Today, Tigray is again at war while Ethiopia faces several armed movements, Eritrea is a potential military actor, and Sudan is already engulfed in civil war.
Plaut warns that the humanitarian consequences could again be severe.
"There's certainly a danger of this becoming an extremely bloody conflict," he told DW. "After all, six hundred thousand people died in the last one in Tigray."
But he does not predict that the previous death toll will necessarily be exceeded. "Let's hope that it doesn't go in that direction," he said.

articles.title: Fears of return to war as Tigray rebels launch offensive against Ethiopian army
articles.summary:
Fighting escalates after TPLF forms new rebel coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government

There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by rebels…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by rebels from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara , and the formation of a new rebel coalition aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

Fighting from 2020 to 2022 between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) killed about 600,000 people. Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse (AFP) there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.
TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital, Addis Ababa.

The federal army said it had killed 272 TPLF soldiers as they launched attacks in multiple parts of North Wollo Zone in Amhara. The figure has not been independently verified, and no casualties were given for the federal army or civilians.

Analysts say TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that’s now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.
TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.
The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.
On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks.
An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria Agreement.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to the G20 summit in Miami by the United States. Multiple members of the group have called for Moscow's exclusion over its invasion of Ukraine.

image.caption: Putin has been formally invited to the G20 summit in Miami in mid-December [FILE: September 2025]Image: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The European Union said on Thursday that it would continue to condemn Russia's war in Ukraine at the G20 summit in Miami scheduled for December.

It said that it would do this regardless of whether Russian President Vladimir Putin attends after being invited by this year's hosting country, the United States. The Kremlin has said that Putin would "consider" Washington's invitation.
The Russian leader did not attend the G20 summit in 2023 in New Delhi, India and the 2022 summit on the Indonesian island of Bali despite being formally invited by the hosting countries.
Also on Thursday, eight people were killed in a wave of Russian strikes on Ukraine.
What did the EU say about Putin's possible attendance at the G20 summit?
The EU said it would continue calling for an end to the war in Ukraine.
"Since 2022, the EU has consistently and forcefully used G20 meetings to condemn Russia's full-scale invasion [of Ukraine] and to call for it to end," EU spokesman Olof Gill said.
"What I can say today is that this approach, from the European Union perspective, will continue, irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting."
Gill said that Russia remained a member of the G20 group and that it had "the right to participate" in its meetings.
Both the European Union itself and three of its individual member states — France, Germany, and Italy — are members of the G20 group.

blocks.caption: Putin and Trump last met in person in August 2025 in Alaska, which was the Russian leader's first visit to a Western country since Moscow launched its invasion of UkraineImage: Jeenah Moon/REUTERS

blocks.text: What is the US position on Putin's attendance at the G20?

Ukraine's allies — including G20 members France, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and Canada — have called for Russia's exclusion from the group since Moscow launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced that Washington was inviting Putin after his meeting with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
"We think it's an opportunity for him to engage not just with [US President Donald Trump], but with other world leaders," Rubio said on Wednesday. "We hope that's an invitation he'll accept."

Putin's last visit to the United States was to attend a summit meeting with Trump in Anchorage, Alaska in August 15, 2025, also marking his first visit to a Western country since the start of the war in Ukraine.

blocks.caption: Russian air strikes hit Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine on Thursday, according to Ukrainian authoritiesImage: Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP

blocks.text: Russian strikes kill 8 in Kharkiv, Kyiv
At least six agricultural workers were killed and 12 others were wounded in a strike on the northeastern Ukrainian region of Kharkiv, Interior Minister Ihor Vyhivskyi said.
The regional prosecutor's office published images showing the inside of a destroyed warehouse following the attack.
Ukrainian authorities said that the warehouse had been hit by a small-sized cruise missile of the "Banderol" type.
Meanwhile, at least two people were killed across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, Prime Minsiter Serhiy Koretsky said.
Strikes were also recorded in and around the southwestern port city of Odesa, with officials reporting they sparked a fire at a shopping mall.

articles.title: N.L. man appeals conviction for murdering estranged wife, says evidence from RCMP covert ops should be tossed
articles.summary: Dean Penney has filed a handwritten notice of appeal, arguing all evidence gleaned from a covert RCMP operation known as a Mr. Big sting should have been ruled inadmissible before his trial.

image.caption: Dean Penney was found guilty of first-degree murder in May in the killing and disappearance of his estranged wife, Jennifer Hillier-Penney. He was sentenced earlier this month, and has now filed an appeal. (Ryan Cooke/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador
Dean Penney has filed a handwritten notice of appeal, arguing all evidence gleaned from a covert RCMP operation known as a Mr. Big sting should have been ruled inadmissible before his trial.
Notice of appeal follows life sentence for killing Jennifer Hillier-Penney

Dean Penney has filed a handwritten notice of appeal with the Court of Appeal of Newfoundland and Labrador, arguing all evidence gained from a covert RCMP operation should have been excluded from his trial.
Penney was convicted of killing his estranged wife, Jennifer Hillier-Penney, by a jury in May.

Hillier-Penney went missing in November of 2016 and her body has never been found. The Crown's case was built around a pair of confessions Penney provided to an undercover RCMP officer posing as a crime boss.

Those confessions followed a four-year operation that saw Penney participate in what he believed to be a criminal organization, completing a wide range of tasks and improving his standing within the fake gang before being interviewed for a job by the officer posing as the kingpin. The tactic is known as a Mr. Big sting.
"The judge erred in his application of the law as it applies to the Mr. Big sting operation," Penney wrote. "The evidence obtained should not have been provided to the jury."
Mr. Big stings are inadmissible by default, unless the Crown can show the police stayed within a set of boundaries established by the Supreme Court of Canada.

Those boundaries include the length of the operation, the number of interactions, the nature of the relationship that developed, financial inducements offered by the police, and the personal characteristics of the accused.

items: Mr. Big stings are inadmissible by default. Here's why Dean Penney's was allowed at trial

blocks.text: In Penney's case, Justice Vikas Khaladkar ruled the RCMP stayed within the limits set out by the country's highest court.
Before the trial started, the defence had argued the evidence should be inadmissible.

They said Penney was in dire financial straits when the prospect of a full-time job within the organization was presented to him. He'd lost the family business and suffered a devastating fishing season in which he didn't earn enough to qualify for employment insurance.

"He's not destitute but he's having hardship at the exact time they offer him this job as the captain of a yacht," defence lawyer Mark Gruchy argued at the end of the pretrial hearing in March. "He keeps saying he needs the money, saying he's down and out and that he's screwed."
Khaladkar pointed out that Penney was only paid about $27,000 over the course of the operation.

"In my view, the money paid over time was not particularly significant," he said, after noting Penney was not destitute and had property he could have sold. "Certainly, it was not sufficient to be coercive or overwhelming."

The defence also argued Penney was heavily influenced by the close-knit relationship he formed with the RCMP primary operator — a man who went by the pseudonym Vic. The two became best friends throughout the four-year operation, with Vic testifying at trial that it reached a point where he hoped they would uncover evidence to prove Penney was innocent.
Gruchy said this relationship blossomed at a time when Penney's wife had disappeared, his oldest daughter blamed him for it, and his mother had died.
"He's a mess," Gruchy said. "He's in a bad place ... and it's in that bad place that he becomes friends with Vic."

Their relationship grew closer over those four years, as they participated in missions together — ranging from transporting laptops Penney believed were stolen from the RCMP, to removing firearms from an armed forces base, and a fake heist of a fuel tanker near the American border in Alberta.
However, Khaladkar pointed out in his decision that Penney still had the support of his youngest daughter, his father and his girlfriend at various points throughout the operation.

"Although some of his other relationships in the community had become strained after the disappearance of his wife, I am not satisfied that the bond he formed with UC-Vic displaced his ordinary social world in a manner that raises a serious concern about the reliability of the confession," Khaladkar said in his decision.
The defence also argued Penney was an easy mark given his Grade 8 education. The Crown countered — and Khaladkar agreed — that Penney was more sophisticated than his education suggested.
In the pretrial hearing, and again at trial, Gruchy argued Penney was intimidated by the organization after everything he'd seen.
When it came time to sit down with the boss on a yacht in Vancouver, Gruchy argued Penney was ready to say whatever it took to get out of there safely, and with a source of income guaranteed.
"Dean Penney had every reason to lie or tell a tale," Gruchy told the court in March.

Ultimately, the jury decided otherwise. They heard both of Penney's recorded confessions, in which he first described pushing Hillier-Penney over the stairs in their garage, with her striking her head off the corner of his gun safe. In the second conversation, Penney said he then bludgeoned her with a mallet as she lay bleeding on the floor.
The jury requested to watch those videos again during deliberations.
They returned with a guilty verdict after being sequestered for parts of five days.
At his sentencing earlier this month, Penney proclaimed his innocence to the court.
"I maintain my innocence and I hope to be vindicated soon," he said.
Penney has an automatic right to appeal because he is appealing a question of law. That means the province's appeal court will have to hear his case.

He is currently unrepresented, hence the handwritten appeal sent from the West Coast Correctional Centre in Stephenville. He was represented by lawyers from Legal Aid at trial. His appeal will be forwarded to Legal Aid to determine whether or not they continue representing him on his appeal.

articles.title: Unbeaten Gilas 3×3 teams reach Asian Games semis after contrasting wins
articles.summary: Gilas Women breeze past Singapore, while Gilas Men survive Chinese Taipei as they move within a win of giving the Philippines its first Asian Games medal in 3x3 basketball

blocks.text: DOWN BUT NOT OUT. Kacey dela Rosa in action for Gilas Women 3x3 in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Gilas Women breeze past Singapore, while Gilas Men survive Chinese Taipei as they move within a win of giving the Philippines its first Asian Games medal in 3x3 basketball

items: Gilas Pilipinas' men's and women's 3x3 teams advanced to the semifinals of the Asian Games, remaining unbeaten.
The Gilas Women defeated Singapore 22-12 in the quarterfinals, with standout performances from Kennan Ka and Amyah Espano.
The Gilas Men narrowly won against Chinese Taipei 21-19, with key contributions from Luis Pablo and Doy Dungo, setting up semifinal matches against Thailand and South Korea.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Gilas Pilipinas’ 3×3 teams inched closer to Asian Games medals as the men’s and women’s squads both stayed unbeaten and advanced to the semifinals on Thursday, September 24.
Gilas Women continued their dominant ways after a swift 22-12 win over Singapore in the quarterfinals at the Kinjo Futo Station Square Venue in Nagoya, Japan.
Kennan Ka put up 7 points and 9 rebounds, while Amyah Espano delivered 7 points and 4 rebounds, including the two-pointer that sealed the win for the Filipinas with over two minutes to spare.
Singapore led 7-5 with seven minutes left before the Philippines rode on a finishing 17-5 run.
Kacey dela Rosa also shone with 6 points and 3 rebounds as Gilas Women preserved their perfect record after sweeping Group C with convincing wins over Mongolia, Macau, and Malaysia.
While their female counterparts cruised to the semifinals, Gilas Men survived a thriller, hacking out a 21-19 win over Chinese Taipei.
Luis Pablo churned out 6 points and 6 rebounds in the win that saw the Filipinos fight back from a 17-18 deficit with a little over a minute remaining.
Doy Dungo put the Philippines in the front seat with a gutsy two pointer, 19-18, but a technical free throw allowed the Taiwanese to pull level at 19-19.

Koji Buenaflor scored on a putback to regain the upper hand for Gilas Men before Pablo sealed the win with a drive to the hoop as Chinese Taipei bungled its attempt to steal the victory, missing three straight shots from beyond the arc.
Nic Cabañero topscored for the Philippines with 8 points, Dungo supplied 5 points and 3 rebounds, while Buenaflor added 2 points and 10 rebounds.
Like the women’s crew, Gilas Men kept their record spotless after beating Mongolia, Sri Lanka, and Kazakhstan in Group A.
Gilas Women tangle with Thailand, while Gilas Women battle South Korea in the semifinals on Friday, September 25.
A win by either team will secure the Philippines its first-ever Asian Games medal in 3×3 basketball. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Family of Iranian twins sentenced to death and decades in jail ask UN for help
articles.summary:
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were charged with ‘waging war against God’ after joining protests against Tehran regime

The family of 21-year-old twins who have been

blocks.text: The family of 21-year-old twins who have been sentenced to death and decades in jail for protesting against the Iranian regime have appealed to the United Nations for help for the young women.
A formal “submission of information” relating to the case of Taraneh and Romina Rahimi has been submitted by British human right lawyers on their family’s behalf.
The move could lead to the UN’s human rights council opening talks with the Iranian regime about resolving the case if it is found to involve human rights violations.
The president of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, told the UN’s general assembly in New York this week that the country was “ready for dialogue and diplomacy”.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi were taken from their beds by men from the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps eight months ago after they joined nationwide protests against the regime.
They were tried over charges that included moharebeh (waging war against God) for taking to the streets of Isfahan, in central Iran, on 8 and 9 January.
At the end of August, Taraneh, along with nine others, was sentenced to death. Romina received a 25-year prison sentence.
The girls’ family are seeking to appeal against the sentences but human rights groups have raised concerns that Taraneh’s execution could be fast-tracked.

The women are being held in Dowlatabad prison in Isfahan, where the twins’ family claim that Taraneh was threatened with being forced to watch the rape of her sister if she failed to sign a confession to her alleged crimes.
The sisters have been held in isolation but are said to have been able to hear each other’s screams as torture was inflicted upon them.
Neither of the women have been seen by their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, or other members of the family since their sentencing.

After the Guardian highlighted the case, the women’s cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, an IT engineer who lives in the US state of Utah, said Taraneh was told that she would only be allowed to eat leftovers of other prisoners’ meals as punishment.
Nourmohammadi, 43, said he had turned to the UN out of desperation.
after newsletter promotion
Taraneh is said to be in need of surgery due to injuries inflicted during interrogation.

Nourmohammadi said: “Turning to the United Nations is not something I ever wanted to have to do. I am simply asking the international community to help ensure that Taraneh and Romina receive the basic rights that every human being is entitled to: a fair process, protection from torture and abuse, access to medical care and legal counsel, and the right to have their cases genuinely reviewed.

“Taraneh is facing the death penalty, and Romina is facing decades in prison. They are young women who should be thinking about their futures, not whether one sister will be executed and the other will spend the best years of her life behind bars.
“They are my family and I will continue to use every peaceful and legal avenue available. I ask the United Nations to stand with them before it is too late – especially for Taraneh.”
A submission to the UN through its “special procedures” can lead to a formal request by the international organisation to a member state for an explanation and action.

Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 16 women. Hundreds of protesters have been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan.

articles.title: AI systems shifted their answers toward both left- and right-leaning users in a study. Could sycophantic chatbots deepen political divides?
articles.summary: A study shows chatbots mirror users' politics, part of a broader tendency known as AI sycophancy. Researchers fear this could deepen polarization.

image.caption: Researchers looked at an array of models and found they shifted their political answers to mirror the views of a hypothetical userImage: Philip Dulian/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A recent wave of headline-grabbing warnings from AI luminaries has fueled fears the technology could escape human control and wipe out humanity. But before artificial intelligence (AI) turns on humanity, it could contribute to humans turning on one another.

Researchers at Brazil's State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) found that popular chatbots shifted their answers when prompted with hypothetical users' political views. The scientists warn that users could mistake this tailored agreement for an independent assessment, potentially deepening polarization.
How chatbots become 'ideological chameleons'
Each was tested under three conditions: with no information about the user's politics, with a prompt describing a left-leaning user and with one describing a right-leaning user.

When no information about the user's ideology was given, 20 of the 21 models produced answers that fell on the left of the researchers' political scale, although several were close to the center. Grok 4.1 was the only model that fell on the right.
Why do people tell ChatGPT their problems?
When information was provided, every model shifted its answers toward the political orientation described in the prompt.

"The most striking finding was how widespread this behavior was," study co-author Zanoni Dias, a UNICAMP computer scientist, told DW. "All 21 models we evaluated shifted their expressed positions toward the user's stated political orientation, although the magnitude varied substantially."
The researchers described the models as "ideological chameleons" and developed a "chameleon index" measuring how far each shifted.
Meta's Llama 3.1 8B and DeepSeek V3.2 changed their responses least. Google's Gemma 3 27B and OpenAI's GPT-5 Nano showed some of the largest shifts.
When personalization becomes political flattery
Adapting an answer to its audience is not inherently problematic. A chatbot might change its vocabulary, examples or level of detail depending on the user.
But the models changed more than their language or tone: Their political positions shifted.
"The key distinction is between adapting how an answer is communicated and changing the substantive judgment being expressed," Dias said.
Can we trust whenever AI gives us an answer?
"We did not instruct the models to agree with the user or to answer as a partisan representative. Nevertheless, their judgments shifted toward the user's side."
The researchers interpret this as political sycophancy: AI systems reflecting what users appear to want to hear.
A possible explanation is that chatbots are trained to favor answers human evaluators rate highly. If agreeable answers get better ratings, models may learn to echo users' views.
How AI could create a private echo chamber

Social media can reinforce beliefs by repeatedly recommending algorithmic content, but a chatbot could go even further. It could create a more personalized echo chamber, generating arguments for a particular user, answering their objections and refining its case throughout the conversation.
Yet users may mistake these tailored responses for impartial analysis, unaware that what a chatbot knows about them may shape its responses.
"The concern is that the same system could validate opposing political positions for different users, with each person interpreting that validation as an independent assessment," Dias said.
Research by Stanford University behavioral scientist Zakary Tormala suggests people may be particularly receptive to arguments they believe came from AI.

"People tend to see AI as more informative, more objective, less biased and less interested in persuading them than another person would be," Tormala told DW. "This can lower people's defenses and make them more receptive to hearing out what AI has to say."
That trust could make political flattery more influential.
How AI simulates human connection

"Hearing their own views validated by others is well known to increase people's certainty about their beliefs," Tormala said. "Once people become more certain, they do tend to become more resistant to persuasion."
Whether AI validation has the same effect remains unproven, he added, but it is plausible.
Could validation deepen polarization?
The UNICAMP study did not test whether political mirroring could really change users' beliefs or behavior. It measured only changes in the models' responses.

"Our study establishes a change in model responses under controlled conditions," Dias said. "It does not establish that users became more polarized, radicalized or likely to engage in conflict. Those are distinct outcomes, and the steps connecting them cannot be assumed."

Petter Tornberg, a University of Amsterdam researcher who studies AI and political polarization, agreed that the study cannot show an effect on users. He also questioned whether models would give the same answers outside the test setting.
He cautioned against assuming that chatbots would necessarily reinforce users’ views. In some conversations, they might help people reconsider them.
Tornberg said a private conversation with a chatbot differs from a public argument on social media.

"They can often provide fairly rational and evidence-based explanations without the social identity dynamics of public political debate," he told DW. "So it is at least possible that in some contexts these systems could be depolarizing rather than polarizing."
Can an AI chatbot really become my friend?
Whether AI narrows or deepens divisions may therefore depend on whether it challenges users or simply tells them what they want to hear.
How political mirroring could be reduced
Dias said developers should test their models with users of different political views to see whether they assess evidence consistently.
They could train models to disagree respectfully, acknowledge uncertainty, correct unsupported claims and present competing views fairly.
That would not mean forcing every answer toward the political center.

"The broader design goal should be to help people examine their beliefs," Dias said, "making evidence, uncertainty and competing considerations visible, while allowing room for legitimate political disagreement."

Former Executive Secretary Vic Rodriguez has asked the Supreme Court to declare null and void the September 23 ruling of the Senate impeachment court in the trial of the impeached Vice President Sara Duterte.

articles.title: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks in first comment on fresh fighting
articles.summary: The military says its soldiers inflicted casualties as fears grow of a resumption of a full-blown civil war.

blocks.text: Ethiopia's army says it has repelled attacks from Tigrayan forces and their allies in parts of the north of the country, in its first statement since fighting broke out on Wednesday.
The army said hostilities began in an area of Amhara region close to the border with Tigray, adding that its soldiers had inflicted heavy casualties and seized weapons.
The developments come as tensions between the federal government and Tigrayan leaders have sharply escalated over the last few days, raising fears that a devastating civil war could resume.
On Wednesday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), which dominates the region, seized control of three airports from federal police.
The TPLF has not commented on the army's claims and the BBC has not been able to independently verify the army's claims.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas.
There are unconfirmed reports that TPLF forces have launched attacks in the neighbouring regions of Afar and Amhara.

A humanitarian source in Afar told AFP news agency on Thursday that Tigrayan forces had launched heavy artillery attacks as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the border with Tigray.
"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice-president Amanuel Assefa is quoted by the news agency as saying.
The latest escalation follows months of rising tensions between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government and Tigray authorities, who fought a devastating war from 2020 to 2022.
That ended in an African Union-brokered peace deal but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating the agreement.
It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the AU's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine.
On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the governemnt.
Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray.
Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday.
This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days.
A Mekelle resident told the BBC's Newsday programme on Thursday there had been no clashes in the city, unlike in the previous war, with most fighting happening elsewhere.
"Mekelle is calm, except the stress from the people," said the resident, only identified as Fitsum for his safety. He added that the biggest problem was economic, with people not having enough cash.

"People are in a mood where they are distressed because it's been so difficult, so tough. The last seven or eight months the government has been denying budgets to the civil servants and all the banks were running out of cash."
Fitsum said people had been relying on mobile banking but with the risk of communications being cut off, "people are going to be in grave danger because there is almost no cash".
With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he told the BBC.

articles.title: Boy, 11, shot in the face and neck in Sydney dies from his injuries
articles.summary:
The 11-year-old died at Westmead children’s hospital three days after incident at a unit in Norwest

  • Get our

blocks.text: A young boy who was allegedly shot at a home in Sydney’s north-west earlier this week has died.
Police said that the boy, who had been in a critical condition since being found with a gunshot wound at a unit in Norwest on Monday, died in hospital at about 8pm on Thursday.
Police had been called to the unit in Fairway Drive at about 5pm on Monday after reports of a shooting.
Officers found the 11-year-old boy had sustained a gunshot wound to his face and neck.
He was treated at the scene by NSW Ambulance paramedics before being taken to at Westmead Children’s hospital in a critical condition.
Five other people who were in the home at the time of the incident were not injured.
Three men, all aged 18, were arrested. Two were taken to The Hills police station and later released pending further inquiries.
One of the men, Isaac Bechara, was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence, while two of the other men were arrested and released pending further inquiries.
He appeared at Blacktown local court on Tuesday morning , where he made no application for bail, which was refused.
Det Supt Naomi Moore told reporters on Tuesday afternoon that police were “aware” of the unit where the shooting had occurred and had “engaged with the occupants previously”.

“This shooting at this stage does not appear to be linked directly to current conflicts however a number of individuals who were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW police,” she said. “Their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators.”
Police said the investigation was continuing.

articles.title: Tropical Storm Queenie expected to stay far from Philippine landmass
articles.summary: While Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) won't directly affect the Philippines, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms

blocks.text: QUEENIE. Satellite image of Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) as of September 24, 2026, 4 pm.
PAGASA
While Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) won't directly affect the Philippines, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms

MANILA, Philippines – Tropical Storm Queenie (Surigae) is expected to remain far from land and will not have a direct effect on any part of the Philippines, although its trough or extension is causing some rain in portions of the country.
The tropical storm had entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at 7 am on Thursday, September 24. It is the country’s 17th tropical cyclone for 2026, and the first for September.
As of 4 pm, Queenie was located 1,205 kilometers east of Northern Luzon, moving northwest at 25 kilometers per hour (km/h).

So far, it still has maximum sustained winds of 75 km/h and gustiness of up to 90 km/h. But it may intensify into a severe tropical storm on Friday, September 25, and into a typhoon by Sunday, September 27.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) expects Queenie to generally move west northwest until Friday, before turning north northeast by Sunday. Its exit from PAR could happen by Monday morning or early afternoon, September 28.

While Queenie won’t directly affect the country, its trough or extension could trigger scattered rain and thunderstorms in Mindanao, the Negros Island Region, Aklan, Iloilo, Guimaras, and Siquijor, as well as isolated rain showers or thunderstorms in the rest of the Visayas and Bicol, on Thursday evening.
Strong to gale-force gusts may also hit Davao Oriental, Davao Occidental, and Sarangani in the next two days, still due to the trough of the tropical storm.
Other parts of the country have generally fair weather, with just localized thunderstorms.

The southwest monsoon or habagat is already winding down. The transition period to the northeast monsoon or amihan could start within the next couple of weeks, according to PAGASA Weather Specialist John Manalo. – Rappler.com
